source.title: Multilingual Language Models Encode Script Over Linguistic Structure
source.citation: Aastha A. K. Verma et al., 2026
source.authors: Aastha A. K. Verma; Anwoy Chatterjee; Mehak Gupta; Tanmoy Chakraborty

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures and intervenes on language-associated neurons and SAE features, but does not test whether neuron poles have one or two human-nameable jobs, whether explanations predict held-out activations, or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper's own LAPE, overlap, probing, and ablation results concern language-associated units and their sensitivity to script or word order. They do not measure the share of poles with a main job or test explanations of neurons. Prior-work results cited in the paper are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper identifies language-associated MLP neurons and SAE features with LAPE and measures how stable they are under romanization and word shuffling, probes them for typology, and ablates them. It never audits how many neuron poles have one main job, never scores neuron explanations against held-out activations, and builds no attribution graphs. It mentions in passing that raw neurons are 'typically denser and more polysemantic', but that is an assertion, not a measurement. None of its results bear on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Accurate. The authors conclude that language-associated units are organized mainly around surface form, especially script; typology becomes more accessible with depth; and generation depends most on units invariant to surface perturbations.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LAPE and SAE-LAPE to identify language-associated raw neurons and SAE features, then tests script and word-order perturbations, typological probes, and causal ablations. It does not use the claimed pole-job audit or explanation-on-held-out-activations procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with script versus word-order perturbation, raw neurons versus SAE features, language, and layer. Romanization causes low overlap; shuffling generally preserves overlap, with selective instability in SAE features for some Latin-script languages.

fits_no_version.finding: In Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, language-associated units from romanized inputs overlap little with native-script units and almost not at all with English units. This holds for raw neurons and SAE features, and persists at 8B/9B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-associated units in multilingual LMs are strongly conditioned on script rather than on abstract language identity.

fits_no_version.finding: Word-order shuffling largely preserves which language-associated units are selected; some Latin-script languages show reduced overlap in SAE features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The identity of language-associated units is robust to word-order perturbation.

fits_no_version.finding: Typological properties become linearly decodable at different depths: genealogy early, phonology in late layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Typological structure becomes more accessible with model depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating shuffle-invariant overlap neurons degrades perplexity more than matched random controls. Mean-replacing only-native neurons causes large perplexity shifts and language switching.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-associated neuron subsets defined by invariance to perturbation differ in causal importance for generation.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper analyzes MLP activations and their SAE decompositions, not attention heads or embeddings. The main exposition centers on 1B and 2B models, with scaling validation only up to 9B. Several overlap and probing results are summarized qualitatively or presented in figures without exact values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Supplementary distributions, additional per-language overlap plots, Gemma causal-ablation tables, and Llama-3-8B causal-ablation tables are not separately cataloged here; they concern the same adjacent language-associated-unit findings and do not test any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No audit of neuron-pole job shares in Qwen3-32B or any model.
Covers Llama/Gemma models from 1B to 9B, but only for language-unit overlap; no interpretable-share measurement, no MoE models, nothing at trillion scale.
No vision models; no analysis of canonical polysemantic neurons or pose.
No estimate of interpretable-neuron share as a function of tools or architecture.
No attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.
No explanations from activating examples tested on held-out activations.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the relation from 'discusses' to 'cites_only' because the paper never engages with the neurons-are-clean claim; 'discusses' would also be defensible, and T6 is correct either way. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The row states describe the paper's own effects, not any version, so they need no fixes for verdict purposes.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit the share of neuron poles with one job, two related jobs, or unknown jobs in Qwen3-32B.
Tests language-associated-unit behavior across some model families and sizes, but not the claimed shares of interpretable neuron poles or models up to trillions of parameters.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares in InceptionV1-sized vision models or test the proposed architecture, regularization, or tools explanation.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether neurons suffice as circuit units without a replacement model.
Does not test explanations written from activating examples against held-out activations.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B
rows.operation_detail: Compared Jaccard overlap of language-associated raw neurons from romanized inputs with native-script units.

conditions.value: Across languages; Spanish has higher overlap

rows.value: Overlap remains consistently low, typically below 0.3; higher overlap only for Spanish, which already uses the Latin script.
rows.note: The reported comparison concerns language association, not the number of interpretable jobs per neuron.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B

rows.value: Overlap peaks around layer 9 at Jaccard ≈ 0.3 and never approaches convergence.

rows.note: The paper describes a modest mid-layer increase but persistent separation.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B

rows.value: Languages with distinctive scripts remain highly stable, often exceeding 0.7; several Latin-script languages have somewhat reduced overlap in SAE features.
rows.note: The study reports selective instability by language and representation.

rows.subject: Llama-3.2-1B

rows.value: Genealogical properties are accessible from early layers; more abstract phonological features emerge mainly in the deepest layers.
rows.note: This measures linear accessibility of typological properties, not single-neuron job interpretability.
